analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans road-building and logging in undeveloped roadless areas of national forests.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 21 Democratic and independent cosponsors, never got a hearing or vote; it died in the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would turn the 2001 Roadless Rule from an agency regulation into federal law, barring the Department of Agriculture from allowing road construction, road reconstruction, or logging in inventoried roadless areas of the national forests. The bill's findings say these areas supply drinking water to tens of millions of Americans, support hunting, fishing, and outdoor recreation, and save downstream communities money on water filtration. It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee on the day it was introduced and never received any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Households whose drinking water comes from national forest watersheds, hikers, hunters, anglers, and communities with recreation-based economies. The bill's findings say roadless areas provide clean water for domestic and agricultural use, drinking water for tens of millions of citizens, backcountry fish and game habitat, and jobs and consumer spending in recreation economies. Downstream communities also save millions in water filtration costs, according to the bill.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Water users, hunters, anglers, recreation towns

how_it_helps.text: Bars the Department of Agriculture from allowing road construction, road reconstruction, or logging in inventoried roadless areas where the Roadless Rule prohibits those activities.
Protects watersheds that provide drinking water to tens of millions of Americans and clean water for domestic, agricultural, and industrial uses.
Saves downstream communities millions of dollars in water filtration costs by keeping the land undisturbed.
Supports hunting, fishing, hiking, and other recreation, and adds reliability to recreation-based economies that depend on road-free public land for jobs and revenue.

Cites Forest Service findings that wildfires are almost twice as likely in roaded areas as in roadless ones, and notes the existing 371,581-mile forest road system already carries a $3.2 billion maintenance backlog that new roads would deepen.

analysis.who_pays: Timber companies and logging-dependent communities lose access to timber in roadless national forest land, and road construction contractors lose work building and rebuilding forest roads. Because the Roadless Rule already exists as a regulation, the bill's immediate on-the-ground effect is modest; its main practical effect is making the protections much harder for a future administration to reverse.
analysis.who_pays_short: Timber companies and forest road builders

drawbacks.text: It restricts timber harvest in roadless national forest areas, eliminating logging opportunities there for the timber industry and communities that depend on timber jobs.

It locks a 2001 management rule into statute, limiting the flexibility of future administrations and forest managers to adjust roadless-area policy, including for Idaho and Colorado where modified rules are grandfathered in.

Supporters would have to acknowledge that because the Roadless Rule is already in force as a regulation, the bill's main benefit is durability rather than new protection — while its main cost, foregone timber and road-building, falls on a concentrated set of rural industries.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are broad and the beneficiaries are diffuse: drinking water, wildlife habitat, and recreation for millions of people, plus savings on water filtration. The costs are real but concentrated — logging and road-building opportunities on a defined set of federal acres — and are mitigated by the fact that the same restrictions already apply under the existing rule. On balance, the bill trades a narrow industrial loss for a wide public benefit, and its main weakness is that it mostly preserves the status quo rather than adding new protection.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Maria Cantwell introduced the bill on May 2, 2019, joined by 18 other senators including Udall, Wyden, Blumenthal, Durbin, Murray, Booker, Harris, Merkley, Warren, Sanders, and Whitehouse.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day.
No further action was ever taken on the bill; the committee never scheduled a hearing or a vote, and the bill never reached the Senate floor.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill expired without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Timber companies and forest road-construction interests are better off, since roadless areas remain open in principle to policy change. The protections stay in place only as an agency rule, which a future administration could modify, rather than as a law only Congress could undo.

sides.party_line_note: All 21 supporters were Democrats or the one independent, Sen. Sanders; no Republicans cosponsored, and the Republican-chaired committee to which it was referred never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill bars logging in inventoried roadless areas of the national forests, removing timber supply the industry can currently access in principle through the regulatory process. Because the Roadless Rule already applies, the immediate loss is limited to the risk that the rule itself might have been relaxed.
The bill bars road construction and reconstruction in roadless areas, eliminating a source of federally funded road-building work.

The bill's findings say statutory protection adds reliability to recreation-based economies that depend on roadless public land for jobs, revenue, and consumer spending, and preserves hunting, fishing, and backcountry access.
